query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the selective oxidation tendency of the X element governs whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms above 900 °C. Alloys with X elements that preferentially form low-strain, well lattice‐matched oxides (e.g., Al2O3 or SiO2) will develop adherent, persistent oxide scales, whereas alloys with X elements leading to higher expansion mismatches (e.g., Mn-oxides) will tend to develop unstable, cracked or spalled scales.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) in either single-phase or multiphase solid-solution states produced under standard processing conditions.
generation.intervention: Exposure to high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative/corrosive atmospheres contrasted against vacuum (inert) thermal treatment, monitored in situ by high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) along with CALPHAD modeling.
generation.conditions: Thermal treatment at temperatures above 900 °C in oxygen-containing (or corrosive) atmospheres compared to inert (vacuum) conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The lattice matching and interfacial structure between the newly formed oxide (e.g., Al2O3 or SiO2 versus Mn-oxide) and the alloy substrate, which influences interfacial stresses and adhesion quality.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism is based on the differential oxidation kinetics: preferential oxidation of the X element occurs. When X forms an oxide with low thermal expansion mismatch and high adhesion (as with Al or Si), a coherent, protective layer develops that retards further oxidation. In contrast, if the dominant oxide (as with Mn) has high volumetric or lattice mismatch with the substrate, stress accumulates during thermal cycling, leading to cracking or spallation of the oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidative exposure at >900 °C, alloys containing Al or Si as the X element will exhibit a stable, coherent oxide scale that persists over time, whereas alloys containing Mn will form oxide layers that crack or spall due to higher interfacial stresses.
generation.baseline: Results from comparable thermal treatments performed in vacuum conditions, where minimal oxidation occurs, serve as the baseline to isolate the effects of oxidation.
generation.boundary: Predicted behavior applies specifically to conditions above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres and for alloys produced with typical high-entropy alloy processing; results at lower temperatures or with modified processing may differ.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences in oxidation kinetics, oxide scale thickness, and spallation thresholds are not precisely defined and may be influenced by additional factors (e.g., minor compositional variations, processing conditions). Further refinement through CALPHAD modeling and in-situ measurements is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Utilize in-situ HTXRD and post-exposure microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) to compare the oxide formation behavior on CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Al, Si, Mn) during thermal exposure above 900 °C in both oxidative and vacuum environments. Use CALPHAD modeling to predict the oxidation kinetics and verify oxide phase formation.
measurements: Oxide scale phase identification via HTXRD
Oxide scale thickness and morphology via microscopy
Lattice parameter measurements to assess interfacial mismatch
Quantification of spallation/crack density on the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If all alloy variants, regardless of the X element, develop oxide scales with similar structural coherence, adhesion, and stability under oxidative conditions, or if the expected differences as predicted by the oxidation kinetics of the X element are not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.
